newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia army told to protect poll from boycotts.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia army told to protect poll from boycotts.

text.p: Indonesian President Suharto on Friday asked the country's powerful armed forces to prevent any disturbances during next month's general election by those calling for a poll boycott.
Suharto told the nation's top military officers, who met this week to discuss plans for safeguarding the poll, that the percentage of eligible voters who cast ballots had been high in past elections.

"Please don't let this high political awareness be disturbed by those who are irresponsible and who want to lead the people astray by urging them not to use their right to vote," Suharto told the officers from the three branches of the military and the police.
"I ask the state security forces to prevent early every disturbance, blockage and threat to the general election, especially those to the security and safety of the nation," he said.
Indonesia goes to the polls on May 29.

Voting is compulsory in Indonesia and voter turnout was about 95 percent at the last poll in 1992. Analysts from the ruling Golkar party estimate only about three percent of voters either deliberately spoiled their ballots or boycotted the poll.

However, a number of student groups and activists have called for a poll boycott since Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) leader Megawati Sukarnoputri was ousted at a government-backed congress last June.
Analysts say the ruling Golkar party helped orchestrate her dismissal out of fear that she was becoming too popular.

Indonesia's three sanctioned political parties on Thursday reached agreement with the government that the official campaign period will begin on April 27 and run to May 23 before a five-day cooling-off period ahead of polling day.
"There is not one group which will benefit from riots, no matter how small," Suharto said.

To reduce the chance of clashes between party supporters, the government has called for a system dividing the country into three campaign zones covering Sumatra, Bali, Nusa Tenggara and East Timor; Java, Maluku and Irian Jaya; and Kalimantan and Sulawesi.
The election schedule says each party will have nine days to campaign in each zone.
Indonesia only allows Golkar, the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) and the Christian-Nationalist PDI to contest elections.
Golkar officials said on Thursday night the ruling party would campaign on Java, where more than 60 percent of the country's population lives, on the first day of the campaign.

The government, fearing further unrest after several recent riots, has this year banned mass outdoor rallies and street parades which were in the past a major feature of election campaigning in Indonesia.
In its place, they have promoted televised campaigning with dialogues, debates and party statements.
Access to national television broadcasts will be rotated each day of campaigning with the PDI having the first day and Golkar the last.

In Indonesia's tightly controlled electoral system, Golkar is almost assured of achieving a landslide victory on May 29 and reaching its target of winning more than 70 percent of the vote, up from around 68 percent at the last poll.
